clinicalPearls: An abnormal additional row of eyelashes emerging from the meibomian gland orifices along the posterior lid margin
These aberrant lashes are often finer and less pigmented and may rub on the cornea causing irritation
It may be congenital, sometimes inherited, or acquired following chronic lid inflammation or cicatrisation
The congenital form is associated with lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome linked to FOXC2 mutations
It should be distinguished from trichiasis, in which normally sited lashes are misdirected
Treatment targets the aberrant follicles with cryotherapy, electrolysis or lid-splitting procedures
reference.pathophysiology: Distichiasis arises when meibomian glands, which are modified sebaceous glands, differentiate abnormally into complete pilosebaceous units that produce lashes from the posterior lid margin. In the congenital form this reflects a developmental abnormality, classically with FOXC2 mutations in lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome, whereas acquired distichiasis follows metaplasia of the glands after chronic inflammation or cicatrising conjunctival disease. The posteriorly placed lashes can abrade the ocular surface, causing irritation and, if chronic, corneal damage.
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination identifying lashes from meibomian orifices
Assessment of corneal involvement with fluorescein
Family history and examination for limb lymphoedema (lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome)
Genetic evaluation where a hereditary syndrome is suspected
Assessment for underlying cicatrising disease in acquired cases
redFlags: Corneal abrasion or scarring threatening vision
Associated lymphoedema suggesting a genetic syndrome
reference.prognosis: Vision is preserved with appropriate follicle-directed treatment, though recurrence can occur; the associated lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome carries its own systemic implications.
pitfalls: Confusing distichiasis with trichiasis, which differ in origin and treatment
Missing lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome and its cardiovascular associations
Simple epilation alone, which is followed by regrowth
management: Definitive treatment directed at the aberrant follicles with cryotherapy, electrolysis, radiofrequency ablation or lid-splitting with cryoablation
Ocular surface protection with lubricant drops and ointment, plus epilation or a bandage contact lens for temporary relief of corneal irritation
Slit-lamp surveillance with fluorescein staining for corneal abrasion and keratopathy
Identify and treat any underlying cicatrising conjunctival disease driving acquired distichiasis
Oculoplastic referral for surgical follicle ablation, with examination for limb lymphoedema suggesting lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome
Genetic counselling and FOXC2 evaluation where hereditary lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome is suspected
